title: Self-testing the toric code against classical communication
authors: Gustavo Fróes, Amanda Wei, Carlos de Gois, Denis Rochette, Marc-Olivier Renou
abstract: Device-independent self-testing certifies a multipartite quantum state from the correlations it produces alone, without assumptions on the inner workings of the devices. Most existing self-tests, however, break down as soon as the parties can exchange messages. We consider a relaxed setting in a quantum network, where in the honest version of the protocol, the parties never communicate, yet certification remains sound even in an untrusted case where the untrusted devices secretly exchange classical messages within a bounded distance in the network. We show that the code space of the toric code, distributed over a network with the geometry of a torus, can be self-tested in this setting in a noise-robust way, against communication up to distances proportional to the network diameter. We also develop an algorithmic method for constructing such protocols and extend our results to the surface code and cluster states, robust to one round of nearest-neighbor classical communication
summary: This paper develops communication-robust self-testing protocols for the toric code, a key model in quantum error correction. It extends existing theory to account for limited classical communication between distant parties in a quantum network. The main result demonstrates that the code space can be verified using measurement statistics even when classical messages are exchanged up to a distance proportional to the network size.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing device-independent self-testing protocols for multipartite quantum states, specifically relaxing the strict requirement that parties cannot communicate classically.
main_result: They successfully show that the code space of the toric code can be self-tested in a noise-robust way even when parties can exchange classical messages within a bounded distance proportional to the network diameter.
method: The authors develop systematic algorithmic methods, involving the analysis of submeasurements and comparison between physical experiment statistics and reference expectations, to certify the required stabilizer properties.
model_or_system: The primary model is the toric code, a topological error-correcting code defined on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions. The analysis is extended to a quantum network setting where communication is possible but restricted.
key_observables: Expectation values of products of Pauli operators ($\langle\Psi| O_i eO_{x_i} |\Psiangle$) measured in a Physical Experiment (PE) compared to a Reference Experiment (RE).
important_parameters: The robustness is quantified by the maximum communication distance $r$, which is shown to be proportional to the network diameter.
main_assumptions: The classical messages exchanged are assumed not to depend on the outcomes of the quantum measurements, and the measurements in the PE are assumed to be projective.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the measurement patterns (certificates) required for self-testing the toric code for increasing rounds of classical communication ($r=2$ through $r=5$), detailing certificates for anticommutation and stabilizer generators.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general concept of self-testing to the specific case of the toric code. It first establishes the necessary conditions for communication-robust protocols, then details the mathematical framework using submeasurements, and finally presents systematic constructions and results for increasing communication distances $r$.
why_interesting: The work provides a powerful generalization of quantum resource certification, showing how topological quantum error-correcting codes can be verified even in realistic, noisy quantum networks where limited classical communication is possible.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the primal and dual loops acting on a patch toric code. Physical qubits are associated with the edges of the primal lattice. The orange paths represent contractible loops in the primal lattice, and the corresponding product of Pauli Z operators. The blue path represents a contractible loop in the dual lattice, and the corresponding product of Pauli X operators act- ing on the primal edges crossed by the loop.

Figure 2: A 3 × 3 patch of the toric code with the inputs given by the referee to each party in the submeasurements 1 through 4, from left to right, for certifying the anticommutation relations without any communication. For (a) a vertical edge and (b) a horizontal edge. Orange and blue loops represent primal and dual contractible loops, respectively. The numbers inside the qubits indicate the corresponding measurement inputs, while the target qubit (a) t = V (2, 1) and (b) t = H(1, 2) is highlighted by a square. Parties without explicit inputs receive 1 and do not participate in the submeasurement.

Figure 3: Communication graph (black dashed lines) for the parties on the toric code lattice (gray lines). The four neighbors of the party located at V (1, 0), shown in black, are highlighted in gray.

Figure 4: A 9 × 9 patch of the toric code showing the inputs assigned by the referee in measurements 1 through 4, ordered left to right and top to bottom, to certify the anticommutation relations. The fine lattice is shown in gray, while the coarse-grained lattice is highlighted in black. Orange and blue curves represent primal and dual contractible loops, respectively. The numbers displayed on the qubits indicate the corresponding measurement inputs, and the target qubit t = V (6, 4) is highlighted by a square.
